stories.title: UK Biobank will search 80,000 stored blood samples for the first protein clues of brain disease
stories.summary: UK Biobank's PRISM study will measure hundreds of brain-related blood proteins in 80,000 stored samples, many given years before a diagnosis, to look for early signs of Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and rare dementias. A study launch funded by the Michael J Fox Foundation, Alzheimer's Research UK and LifeArc; results are due by the end of 2027.

stories.title: An AI reads long health questionnaires to flag possible Parkinson's sooner
stories.summary: Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute's Quest2Dx uses a language model to read health questionnaires, works around skipped answers and outperformed earlier models; a 30-question version was nearly as accurate as the full ones (Nature Aging). It's meant to flag people for earlier testing, not to diagnose, and it still makes false positives and negatives.

stories.title: Thirty people with ALS will test a wearable brain interface for communicating at home
stories.summary: Cognixion is enrolling 30 adults with ALS in its NIH-supported CHOICE study: each uses its non-invasive brain-computer interface with AR glasses, a touchscreen version and their own eye-tracking device at home for 12 weeks. An investigational device, not FDA-cleared; no results yet.

predictions.note: Cognixion is enrolling 30 adults with ALS to test its non-invasive wearable brain interface for communication at home over 12 weeks: a study starting, with no results yet.

stories.title: AI from David Baker's lab designed brand-new enzymes that cut proteins
stories.summary: Generative AI models from Nobel laureate David Baker's lab designed new proteases, enzymes that cut proteins; once a water molecule was modelled in, 31 of 38 metalloprotease designs worked, and some cut human proteins linked to Alzheimer's. A lab study: the best designs were still 10 to 100 times weaker than natural enzymes.

stories.title: Brain scans hint we map emotions on a hexagon grid, the way we map places
stories.summary: Emory University researchers scanned 18 people as they followed faces and phrases moving between emotions and found a sixfold, grid-like pattern in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, like the grid cells that map space (PLOS Biology). A small brain-imaging study; it doesn't show the grid drives how we feel.

stories.title: Anthropic shared FlashProve, a way to prove which AI model wrote an answer
stories.summary: Anthropic's open-source FlashProve research gives a cryptographic proof that an output came from a specific model, checked against a published 'fingerprint' that doesn't reveal the model's weights, so a provider couldn't quietly swap in another model. Research code only: there are no plans to deploy it yet.

stories.title: In early-onset Alzheimer's, tau piles up more than twice as fast
stories.summary: UCSF-led tau PET scans of 390 people whose Alzheimer's began before 65 and 211 with later onset found tau, the protein that tangles inside neurons, built up at more than twice the rate and spread more widely in the younger group (Science Translational Medicine). An imaging study that may explain faster decline; no treatment was tested.

stories.title: A sulfur compound more than doubled the grip of an ageing muscle-repair signal, in lab tests
stories.summary: Kyushu University found a trisulfide compound, LASSS, made 'Super HGF': the signal that wakes muscle stem cells bound its receptor more than twice as strongly in lab tests, and in mice the compound cut the age-type damage that weakens it (Scientific Reports). Lab and mouse work; no muscle-healing result yet.

stories.title: In a 61-person trial, a multi-ingredient supplement improved blood-vessel markers over six months
stories.summary: In the University of Surrey's randomised STAMINA trial, 33 people took the NOVOS Core supplement and 28 a placebo for six months: blood-vessel function and arterial stiffness improved, and systolic blood pressure ended 6.1 mmHg lower than placebo (European Heart Journal Open). A small, preliminary trial of markers, not health outcomes.

stories.title: Older Americans with more dangerous-heat days had up to 23% higher dementia risk
stories.summary: A USC study of 28,512 older Americans found those exposed to at least 7.2 days a year with a heat index of 39.4°C or more had a 23% higher risk of dementia than those with almost none, and the link was stronger where air conditioning was scarce (Alzheimer's & Dementia). Observational: a link, not proof that heat causes dementia.

stories.title: One hour of nature a week gets half the possible mental-health boost, a big review found
stories.summary: A University of Hong Kong meta-analysis of green-space research from 1980 to 2025 found one visit or one hour a week brought 50% of the maximum estimated mental-health benefit, about four hours 90% and about eight hours 99% (Journal of Environmental Psychology). Population averages from observational studies.

stories.title: A 12-session online therapy kept pregnancy anxiety from rising in a 268-person trial
stories.summary: In King's College London's randomised RELAX trial of 268 pregnant people with mild to moderate anxiety, 12 short online sessions training more positive readings of everyday situations cut anxiety before and after birth compared with usual care, along with depression and repetitive negative thinking (JAMA Network Open).

stories.title: Retiring didn't make older Australians any lonelier, a Monash study found
stories.summary: Monash University researchers followed 7,434 Australians aged 55 to 75 for nearly two decades in the HILDA survey: loneliness didn't change in the three years before or after retiring, across incomes and jobs. About one in six report high loneliness, which rises from the late 60s. Observational survey data.

stories.title: Doctors warn one-shot gene editing for common conditions needs a much higher safety bar
stories.summary: Two University of Michigan cardiologists write in JAMA Internal Medicine that gene therapies aimed at common problems such as high cholesterol must meet especially demanding safety standards: unlike pills, a permanent edit can't be stopped, and a rare side effect could harm many people if given to millions. An expert perspective, not a new study.

stories.title: A review of 37 studies found social media time barely tracks teen anxiety or depression
stories.summary: Across 37 studies of nearly 80,000 young people aged 10 to 24, time on social media explained less than 1% of the differences in anxiety and depression symptoms (British Journal of Clinical Psychology). Australia's under-16 limits took effect in December 2025. Mostly observational, and it measured time, not harmful content.

stories.title: A robot got a knee-jerk reflex with no electronics at all, and walked
stories.summary: Tohoku University built a purely mechanical module that senses when an artificial muscle stretches too far and contracts it, like the muscle spindles behind our reflexes. It reproduced the knee-jerk in a musculoskeletal robot and, with simple control, let it walk on two legs (Advanced Intelligent Systems). A lab robot demonstration.

stories.title: Honey from Australia's native stingless bees stopped every bacterium tested in the lab
stories.summary: Honey from Tetragonula carbonaria, a small native bee of Australia's east coast, stopped every bacterium it was tested against, including golden staph and E. coli even when diluted more than tenfold, and its propolis hit certain skin fungi hard (PLOS One). Lab tests only: not yet shown to treat infections in people.

stories.title: A Band-Aid-sized ultrasound implant watched blood flow at spinal injuries in real time, in animals
stories.summary: Johns Hopkins Medicine's MUSIC implant, placed over a spinal cord injury during surgery, gave real-time imaging of blood flow around the injury in a first proof-of-concept study in animals (Science Advances). It's meant as a bedside 'mobile MRI' to guide care in intensive care; not yet tested in people.
